extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history; general readers interested in press history and wartime media policy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the procedural, legal, and editorial standards and practices that shaped American newspaper operations and reporting during World War I (accreditation, censorship laws, propaganda practices, camp newspapers, economic/operational responses).

rubrics_metrics.name: A.E.F. correspondent accreditation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: "Correspondents with this American Expeditionary Force were accredited upon the filing of a $2,000 bond and the deposit of $1,000 for maintenance."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once accredited, correspondents "might go and come as they pleased" and could visit front-line trenches alone or even "go over the top." Unaccredited correspondents were sometimes allowed facilities for observation and reporting (to the disgust of those who had followed the rules). Accredited correspondents' stories were transmitted through the Military Intelligence Service censor's office at press headquarters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship of field correspondents by Military Intelligence Service
rubrics_metrics.description: "Their stories all went out through the censor’s office maintained by the Military Intelligence Service at press headquarters."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The censor's office followed the progress of American operations (located successively at five different towns). Major Frederick Palmer wrote the section of U.S. Field Service Regulations dealing with war correspondents and was chief American censor for six months. While censorship created handicaps, after the coming of the A.E.F. procedures became 'sensibly conducted' and most correspondents accepted military restrictions as necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Espionage Act (June 15, 1917) — restrictions on publications
rubrics_metrics.description: The Espionage Act "provided heavy fines and imprisonment for anyone who 'shall wilfully cause or attempt to cause . . . disloyalty ... or shall wilfully obstruct recruiting,' and made publications guilty of such acts unmailable."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There was protracted debate in Congress and the newspapers before passage. Many publishers opposed proposed censorship provisions, but the act became law and was later upheld by the Supreme Court. The statute made it easier for later, severer censorship measures to be passed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trading-with-the-Enemy Act (Oct 6, 1917) — foreign-language and message censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: The Trading-with-the-Enemy Act "authorized censorship of all messages abroad, and required any newspaper or magazine containing articles in a foreign language to file sworn translations with the local postmaster."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision was aimed at the German-language press, sections of which were judged disloyal. The President could issue revocable permits to foreign-language papers freeing them from this requirement during good behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sedition Act (May 16, 1918) — expanded speech restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sedition Act made punishable the writing or publication of "any disloyal, profane, scurrilous, or abusive language about the form of government of the United States, or the Constitution, military or naval forces, flag, or the uniform of the army or navy of the United States," or any language "intended" to bring these things "into contempt, scorn, contumely, or disrepute."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The language of the Sedition Act was broad, allowing wide discretion to administrative agencies. Enforcement involved the Department of Justice and interpretation by the Post Office Department (e.g., treating disloyal papers as unmailable). It led to prosecutions and imprisonment in some cases and contributed to a climate of suppression of radical/socialist and German-language publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post Office enforcement of mailing privileges and judicial deference
rubrics_metrics.description: The Post Office Department interpreted statutes to refuse mailing privileges to papers it believed used language intended to bring the government into disrepute; "No hearing was necessary..." and courts regarded the Postmaster General's decision as conclusive unless clearly wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Post Office could refuse a single issue or assert that missing an issue forfeited a paper's mailing privileges altogether. Publishers seeking injunctions or mandamus faced judicial deference to the Postmaster. The Masses case and many instances of mail refusals (over seventy-five papers affected) illustrate administrative enforcement rather than judicial scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee on Public Information (C.P.I.) voluntary censorship and propaganda practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The C.P.I., set up one week after the declaration of war, was "primarily a propaganda bureau and not a censorship division," but its chairman was a member of the Censorship Board and thus closely tied to enforcement agencies; it presented a voluntary censorship code and issued news releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most papers published all the 6,000 releases from the C.P.I. News Division (including the Official Bulletin). The Advertising Division prepared patriotic advertising copy and coordinated donated or purchased ad space; the C.P.I.'s releases were 'colored with patriotic propaganda' but on the whole accurate and newsworthy. The C.P.I.'s power derived both from official standing and the patriotic desire of the press to support the government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associated Press membership rules influencing consolidations
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules of the Associated Press regarding new memberships "made it virtually impossible to obtain a 'franchise' except by the purchase of a paper that already held one."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These AP rules sometimes occasioned the absorption of weak AP members by financially stronger papers, contributing to consolidation trends in the newspaper industry during and after the war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics and aims of camp and soldiers' newspapers
rubrics_metrics.description: Camp newspapers were "staffed by professional journalists enlisted in the services" and exhibited "an informality, a freedom from the attitudes of strict military discipline, and a robust humor which were distinctively American."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most were weeklies (some dailies or monthlies), distributed free to the men, carried some advertising, and belonged essentially to the men in the ranks, helping to create esprit de corps. Chains like the Y.M.C.A.'s 'Trench and Camp' supplied material; examples include the Stars and Stripes and various unit papers (Radiator, Plane News, Gas Attack).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial standard exemplified by Stars and Stripes
rubrics_metrics.description: Stars and Stripes' "appeal was to the private soldier, and it maintained its hold on him mainly through its honest and often humorous freedom of comment and lack of what the men called 'hokum.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stars and Stripes was an eight-page paper with news, editorials, features, cartoons, and advertising; though controlled by GHQ, it aimed at the private soldier, raised charitable funds from the men, and was governed by an editorial council of experienced newspapermen. The example is presented as a model of successful soldiers' journalism: authenticity, humor, honest comment, and relevance to readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of official government documents as a public-service practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The New York Times "performed throughout the war a great service in the publication of the official documents upon which intelligent opinion might be based. It printed the British and German 'white papers'..." and received a Pulitzer award in 1918 "for the publication in full of so many official reports, documents, and speeches relating to the World War."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making official documents available (sometimes in tabloid form) is presented as a journalistic public service and an editorial choice that can support informed public opinion; the Times' printing of the complete Versailles draft in 1919 is cited as an example of exceptional public-service disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational and economic practices of wartime newspapers
rubrics_metrics.description: War reporting increased page counts ("five to eight pages" of war material), shifted emphasis to evening papers (time-zone advantages gave evening papers a "twenty-five per cent increase in circulation"), and sharply raised costs (cable bills, newsprint, salaries), prompting price increases and consolidation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspapers responded by reducing local/national coverage to make room for war news, raising cover prices (penny papers moved to two cents; Sunday papers rose to ten cents), adopting distribution alternatives to the mails (truck-carrier combinations), and pursuing consolidation to save costs. Government intervention (FTC price-fixing on newsprint, War Revenue Act raising postal rates) also shaped operational responses.
